sources.title: MySQL 8.4 mysqldump — A Database Backup Program
MySQL 8.4 point-in-time recovery using binary log
MySQL 8.4 point-in-time recovery using event positions

claims.text: MySQL 8.4 documents physical backups as raw data-file copies suitable for large databases needing fast recovery, logical backups as portable structure/content representations, and warns that online backups need appropriate locking or equivalent tool mechanisms so concurrent modifications do not compromise backup integrity.

MySQL 8.4 mysqldump documentation states that --single-transaction uses REPEATABLE READ plus START TRANSACTION and gives a consistent state for transactional tables such as InnoDB without long-lived application blocking; only InnoDB tables are guaranteed consistent by this option, while MyISAM or MEMORY tables may change during the dump.

MySQL 8.4 mysqldump documents --source-data with --single-transaction as an online InnoDB backup suitable before PITR: a global read lock is acquired briefly at the beginning, binary-log coordinates are read, the lock is released, and the remainder of the dump is lock free for ordinary reads and writes.

MySQL 8.4 mysqldump documentation explicitly warns that ALTER TABLE, CREATE TABLE, DROP TABLE, RENAME TABLE, and TRUNCATE TABLE during a --single-transaction dump can produce incorrect table contents or binary-log coordinates, or cause the dump SELECT to fail.

MySQL 8.4 defines point-in-time recovery as restoring a full backup and then applying binary-log changes generated after that backup; binary logging must be enabled and the relevant log files must be available, while mysqlbinlog can select events by time or position and applying its output reexecutes represented data modifications.

MySQL 8.4 event-position recovery guidance says to restore the last suitable full backup, use the binlog position recorded by the backup/restore process, inspect mysqlbinlog output to identify the event position before the unwanted operation, and use start/stop positions for application; datetime options are better used to locate positions than as the final applied range.

MySQL 8.4 binary-log documentation distinguishes transactional and nontransactional changes: updates to nontransactional tables are logged immediately and cannot be rolled back through ordinary transaction rollback semantics, so storage-engine mix is a material recovery and validation boundary.

findings: The revised mechanism now binds an InnoDB consistency snapshot to an explicit binary-log coordinate instead of inferring the start point from backup completion time.
Primary MySQL 8.4 mysqldump documentation closes the earlier evidence gap for concurrent DML, nontransactional tables, and DDL during --single-transaction dumps.
The answer distinguishes backup consistency, PITR log continuity, exact stop-position selection, and restore validation as separate failure boundaries.
No material factual claim depends on fabricated production experience or an unsupported universal RPO/RTO value.
